title: Drinking After Donating Blood: How Long to Wait and Why
excerpt: Can you drink alcohol after donating blood? Why the Red Cross says wait 24 hours, what happens if you don't, plasma and platelet donations, and when to get help.
metaDescription: Can you drink alcohol after donating blood? Why the advice is to wait 24 hours, how alcohol raises fainting risk, plasma, and when to see a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The short answer:** wait about 24 hours. The American Red Cross tells donors to avoid alcohol for the 24 hours after giving blood and to drink extra non-alcoholic fluids instead. After a donation your body is down roughly a pint of blood, and alcohol pushes your blood pressure and hydration in the same wrong direction. The real risk isn't long-term damage. It's getting dizzy, fainting, and falling, often hours after you've left the donation center and feel fine.

**The quick rules:** Skip alcohol for the rest of the day and night after donating, and ideally for a full 24 hours. Drink an extra few glasses of water or juice, eat a proper meal, and avoid hard exercise for the rest of the day. If you have an event that evening you can't avoid, wait as long as you can, eat first, sip slowly, stop at one drink, and sit down if you feel off. The same applies after donating plasma or platelets.

> **This is not medical advice.** It's general guidance based on blood-service advice and basic physiology. Always follow the instructions your blood donation center gives you. **Lie down with your feet raised and get help if** you feel faint, sweaty, or sick after donating. **Call 911 or go to an emergency room if** you faint and hit your head, have chest pain, trouble breathing, or a racing or irregular heartbeat, become confused, or have bleeding from the needle site that won't stop with firm pressure. Contact your blood center or a doctor if you have arm pain, numbness, tingling, or growing swelling around the needle site.

## Can You Drink Alcohol After Donating Blood?

You can, in the sense that nothing dramatic happens to most people who have a beer the evening after donating. But it's a poor idea, and it's why blood services consistently tell donors to hold off.

A standard whole blood donation takes about a pint (roughly 470 to 500 milliliters). For an average adult, that's around a tenth of total blood volume. Your body handles this well. It pulls fluid from your tissues into your bloodstream, your heart rate and blood vessels adjust, and most donors walk out feeling normal after a snack and a short rest.

What your body is doing in those first hours, though, is quietly compensating. Your blood volume is lower than usual, and your circulation is working to keep blood pressure steady, especially when you stand up. That's the window where alcohol causes trouble. It doesn't change the donation itself. It just makes it harder for your body to keep you upright and steady while it recovers.

So the honest framing is this: drinking after donating is not dangerous in the way mixing alcohol with certain medicines is. It mainly raises the odds of a dizzy spell, a faint, or a fall, and it can make a few drinks hit noticeably harder than you expect.

## Why Alcohol and Fresh Blood Loss Don't Mix

There are four overlapping reasons, and they all point the same way.

### 1. Both lower your blood pressure

After you donate, your blood vessels tighten a little to keep pressure up with less blood in circulation. Alcohol does the opposite. It relaxes and widens blood vessels, which is why people often look flushed and feel warm after drinking. Widened vessels plus less blood to fill them means lower blood pressure, and lower blood pressure means less blood reaching your brain when you stand up quickly. That's the classic recipe for a head rush or a faint.

### 2. Alcohol drains fluid you're trying to replace

Alcohol suppresses vasopressin (also called antidiuretic hormone), the hormone that tells your kidneys to hold on to water. With less of it, you pass more urine than you drink in. In the hours after a donation, your body is trying to rebuild the fluid part of your blood (plasma) from the water you take in. Drinking alcohol works against that. Our guide to [whether alcohol dehydrates you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you) explains the mechanism in more detail.

### 3. You may feel the effects sooner

Many donors report that drinks seem to hit them faster after giving blood. This hasn't been carefully studied, and losing one pint probably changes your actual blood alcohol level only modestly, because alcohol spreads through all the water in your body, not just your blood. The bigger factor is how you feel. When your blood pressure is already a little low, the dizziness and unsteadiness from alcohol stack on top of it. Add the fact that many people donate on a light stomach or skip the snack afterward, and alcohol absorbs faster too. Our article on [drinking on an empty stomach](/never-hungover/drinking-on-an-empty-stomach) covers why food matters so much.

### 4. It dulls the warning signs

The early signs of a donation reaction (feeling hot, sweaty, pale, queasy, or lightheaded) are easy to miss or dismiss when you've been drinking. Alcohol also slows your reactions and throws off your balance, so if you do start to feel faint, you're less likely to sit down in time and more likely to fall and hurt yourself.

## How Long After Donating Blood Should You Wait to Drink?

**The standard guidance is 24 hours.** That's what the American Red Cross recommends, and blood services in other countries give broadly similar advice to avoid alcohol for the rest of the day after donating.

Here's roughly what recovery looks like, and why 24 hours is a sensible line:

| Time after donation | What's happening | Alcohol advice |
|---|---|---|
| First few hours | Highest risk of a delayed faint. Blood volume is low and your body is still adjusting. | Avoid completely. |
| Rest of that day and night | Your body is pulling fluid back into your blood from what you eat and drink. | Avoid. Focus on water, juice, and a real meal. |
| After about 24 hours | Plasma (the fluid part of blood) is largely replaced. | Moderate drinking is generally fine if you feel normal. |
| Next several weeks | Red blood cells are being rebuilt. | Keep drinking moderate; eat iron-rich food. |
| Next few months | Iron stores slowly refill. | Heavy drinking won't help recovery; consider asking about iron. |

The fluid comes back quickly. Red blood cells take longer, usually several weeks. Iron, which your body needs to make new red cells, can take months to fully return, especially in people who donate often. A 2015 randomized trial published in *JAMA* found that donors who didn't take iron afterward often needed several months to rebuild their iron stores, while those who took a low-dose iron supplement recovered considerably faster.

None of that means you can't have a drink for months. It means the first 24 hours are when alcohol is most likely to cause a problem, and after that, your normal moderate-drinking habits are generally fine as long as you feel well.

### If you feel off, wait longer

The 24-hour rule assumes a routine donation and a normal recovery. If you felt faint during or after donating, needed extra time in the recovery area, or still feel tired, dizzy, or washed out the next day, give yourself more time before drinking. Feeling normal is a better signal than the clock.

## What If You Can't Avoid Drinking That Evening?

Sometimes the timing just doesn't work out. You donated at a workplace drive at lunch and forgot about the birthday dinner that night. If you're going to drink anyway, you can lower the risk:

1. **Push it as late as possible.** The further from the donation, the better.
2. **Rehydrate hard first.** Drink several extra glasses of water or juice through the afternoon. An electrolyte drink can help too.
3. **Eat a full meal before your first drink.** Food slows alcohol absorption and helps keep your blood sugar steady.
4. **Cap it at one drink, and make it a light one.** Beer or a wine spritzer over shots or strong cocktails.
5. **Sip slowly and alternate with water.**
6. **Stay sitting more than standing,** and stand up slowly.
7. **Don't drive.** Donation plus alcohol is a bad combination behind the wheel, even if you'd normally feel fine after one drink.
8. **Tell someone you're with that you donated today** so they know what's going on if you go pale or wobbly.

If at any point you feel hot, sweaty, queasy, or lightheaded, stop drinking, sit or lie down with your feet up, and drink water.

## Drinking After Donating Plasma or Platelets

The same advice applies, with a slightly different reason behind it.

**Plasma donation** uses a machine (a process called apheresis) that separates your blood, keeps the plasma, and returns your red cells to you. You lose fluid, salts, and proteins rather than red cells. That means dehydration and lightheadedness are the main short-term risks, which is exactly where alcohol does the most harm. Plasma donors often donate more frequently than whole-blood donors, so staying well hydrated and eating enough protein matters even more. Wait 24 hours and drink plenty of water or an electrolyte drink. Our guide on [how to rehydrate after drinking](/never-hungover/how-to-rehydrate-after-drinking) has practical tips that work just as well after a plasma donation.

Some people also notice tingling around the lips or fingers during plasma or platelet donation. That comes from the anticoagulant (citrate) used in the machine, which briefly lowers calcium in the blood. It passes quickly, but it's another reason to give your body a clean, well-fed recovery rather than adding alcohol to the mix.

**Platelet donation** also uses apheresis and returns most of your red cells. You lose less fluid than with whole blood, but the session is longer, and the same lightheadedness risks apply. A 24-hour alcohol-free window is still sensible.

**Double red cell donation** (sometimes called Power Red) removes twice the red cells of a standard donation while returning your plasma. Because you lose more red cells, your oxygen-carrying capacity drops more and recovery takes longer. Be especially careful with alcohol for the first day, and take it easy in the days after.

## Drinking Before Donating Blood

People search this the other way around too, so here's the short version.

- **Don't donate while drunk or hungover.** Donation staff can defer you if you appear intoxicated or unwell, and you'd be taking a pointless risk.
- **A drink or two with dinner the night before** is unlikely to cause a problem for most people, as long as you sleep well, eat breakfast, and drink plenty of water the next morning.
- **Heavy drinking the night before is a bad idea.** A hangover usually means you're dehydrated and short on sleep, and both make fainting during or after donation more likely. You'll also feel worse afterward.
- **Eat a solid, low-fat meal before you go.** The Red Cross advises a healthy meal and avoiding very fatty foods right before donating, because a high-fat meal can affect testing of your donation.
- **Drink extra water beforehand.** The Red Cross suggests an extra 16 ounces (about two glasses) before you donate.

If the main thing on your mind is a blood test rather than a donation, that's a different question. Some blood tests are affected by alcohol, so see our guide to [drinking before a blood test](/never-hungover/drinking-before-blood-test).

## How to Recover Well After Giving Blood

Recovery after a routine donation is simple. These steps help you feel better faster and make it less likely you'll feel faint later:

- **Drink extra fluids.** The Red Cross recommends an extra four 8-ounce glasses of non-alcoholic fluids over the next 24 hours. Water, juice, milk, and electrolyte drinks all count.
- **Eat a proper meal within a few hours.** Something with protein, some salt, and some carbohydrates. The snack at the donation center is a start, not the whole job.
- **Avoid hard exercise and heavy lifting for the rest of the day.** That includes the gym, a long run, or moving furniture. If you usually drink after a workout, our guide on [drinking after a workout](/never-hungover/drinking-after-a-workout) explains why that pairing is already tough on hydration.
- **Keep the bandage on for a few hours,** and avoid heavy carrying with that arm.
- **Stand up slowly** for the rest of the day, especially from a hot bath or shower.
- **Eat iron-rich foods in the following days.** Red meat, poultry, fish, beans, lentils, tofu, leafy greens, and fortified cereals. Eating foods rich in vitamin C at the same meal helps your body absorb iron from plants.
- **Ask about iron if you donate often.** Frequent donors, women of childbearing age, and teenage donors are more likely to run low on iron. Some blood services now suggest a short course of a low-dose iron supplement; ask your doctor or donation center whether that makes sense for you.

### Does alcohol affect iron recovery?

The effect of moderate drinking on iron is complicated, and it isn't a big lever either way for a healthy donor. Long-term heavy drinking is linked to iron problems in both directions, and some drinks with polyphenols (like tea, coffee, and red wine) can reduce how much iron your body absorbs from plant foods when taken with meals. If you're trying to rebuild iron after a donation, it makes sense to keep alcohol moderate and not wash down your iron-rich meals with red wine. Our article on [iron and alcohol](/never-hungover/iron-and-alcohol) goes into this in more depth.

## What a Donation Reaction Looks Like

Knowing the signs helps you act early, which is the whole point of avoiding alcohol in the first place. The most common reaction is a vasovagal reaction: a sudden drop in heart rate and blood pressure that can lead to fainting. It's more common in first-time donors, younger donors, and people with lower body weight or smaller blood volume, but it can happen to anyone.

Early warning signs include:

- Feeling lightheaded, dizzy, or "floaty"
- Suddenly feeling hot or sweaty, or going pale
- Nausea or stomach discomfort
- Blurry or tunnel vision, or ringing in your ears
- Yawning, weakness, or feeling suddenly very tired

Most reactions happen at the donation center, but some happen later, after you've left. That's one reason the advice about alcohol, exercise, and hot showers matters for the rest of the day.

**What to do:** Stop what you're doing and lie down with your feet raised, or sit with your head between your knees. Loosen tight clothing, sip water once you feel steadier, and don't get up until the feeling has fully passed. Then stand up slowly.

## When to See a Doctor

Most post-donation symptoms are mild and pass with rest, fluids, and food. Get medical help in these situations:

> **Call 911 or go to an emergency room if you:**
> - Faint and hit your head, or injure yourself in a fall
> - Have chest pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat, or trouble breathing
> - Become confused or very drowsy, or can't stay alert
> - Have bleeding from the needle site that won't stop after 10 minutes of firm pressure with your arm raised
>
> **Contact your blood center or a doctor soon if you:**
> - Keep feeling dizzy or faint even after resting and drinking fluids
> - Have pain, numbness, tingling, or weakness in the arm or hand
> - Notice swelling or a large, painful, or growing bruise around the needle site
> - Feel unusually tired, breathless, or weak for several days afterward
> - Realize after donating that you have a health or travel detail the donation center should know about

If you had several drinks after donating and someone with you is very drowsy, hard to wake, vomiting while confused, or breathing slowly, treat that as a possible alcohol emergency and call 911. Don't leave them alone to sleep it off. Our [blood alcohol calculator](/never-hungover/blood-alcohol-calculator) can give a rough idea of how much alcohol is in play, but it's no substitute for getting help when something looks wrong.

## Who Should Be Most Careful

Some people have less room for error after donating. Take the 24-hour rule seriously, and think about waiting longer, if you:

- Are a **first-time donor**, or have fainted during or after a donation before
- Are **younger or have a lower body weight**, which means a pint is a bigger share of your blood volume
- Made a **double red cell, plasma, or platelet donation**
- Take **blood pressure medicines** or other drugs that can lower blood pressure or interact with alcohol
- Have been told you have **low iron or borderline hemoglobin**
- Are planning to **drive, work at heights, operate machinery**, or do anything where a sudden faint would be dangerous

If any of these apply and you're not sure what's safe, ask the staff at your donation center before you leave. They answer this question all the time.

## A Note on Hangovers After Donating

If you do drink in the days after donating, keep the basics in mind: eat before you drink, pace yourself, and keep water going alongside. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence, and [electrolytes and alcohol](/never-hungover/electrolytes-and-alcohol) explains when an electrolyte drink is actually worth it.

Some people also use **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and hangovers. Most of the research is from animal and lab studies, with limited human data. It's promising, not proven, and there is no good evidence that it reduces the dizziness or fainting risk after giving blood. It's not a reason to drink sooner after donating. If you want to try it for ordinary nights out once you've recovered, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

## The Bottom Line

Giving blood is safe, and so is moderate drinking, just not on the same afternoon. In the hours after a donation, your body is working to refill the fluid you lost and keep your blood pressure steady, and alcohol undermines both while dulling the warning signs of a faint. Wait about 24 hours, drink extra water, eat a real meal, and skip hard exercise for the day. After that, if you feel normal, you can go back to your usual habits, with a little extra attention to iron-rich food over the next few weeks.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol after donating blood?**

It's best to wait. The American Red Cross advises donors to avoid alcohol for the 24 hours after giving blood and to drink extra non-alcoholic fluids instead. Your body has just lost about a pint of blood, and alcohol lowers blood pressure and pulls water out through your kidneys, which raises the chance of feeling dizzy or fainting.

**How long after donating blood can you drink alcohol?**

The common guidance is to wait 24 hours. By then your body has largely replaced the lost fluid (plasma), so a drink is much less likely to make you lightheaded. Your red blood cells and iron take weeks to months to recover, so keep drinking moderate in the days that follow and eat iron-rich food.

**Does donating blood make you get drunk faster?**

It hasn't been studied well enough to give a number, and the effect on your blood alcohol level from losing one pint is probably modest. The bigger, better-understood problem is that alcohol and blood loss both lower blood pressure, so the same drinks can leave you much more dizzy, wobbly, or faint than usual. Many donors say they feel the effects sooner, so plan for that.

**Can I drink alcohol after donating plasma?**

The same 24-hour wait is a sensible rule. Plasma donation removes mostly fluid, salts, and proteins, so dehydration and lightheadedness are the main risks, and alcohol makes both worse. Drink plenty of water or an electrolyte drink, eat a proper meal, and skip alcohol for the rest of the day and night.

**Can I drink alcohol the night before donating blood?**

A drink or two with dinner is unlikely to be a problem for most people, but heavy drinking the night before is a bad idea. A hangover leaves you dehydrated, which makes fainting more likely, and you should never show up to donate while still feeling the effects of alcohol. Staff can turn you away if you seem unwell or intoxicated.

**What happens if I already had a drink after donating blood?**

For most people, one drink after donating causes no lasting harm. Stop there, drink water, eat something, and sit or lie down if you feel lightheaded. If you feel faint, lie down with your feet raised. Get medical help if you actually faint and hurt yourself, have chest pain or trouble breathing, or the dizziness doesn't settle after resting.

**Why does the Red Cross say no alcohol after donating?**

Because the most common problem after giving blood is feeling faint, and alcohol works in the same direction. It widens blood vessels, lowers blood pressure, makes you pass more urine, and dulls your judgment and balance. Together with the fluid you just lost, that raises the chance of a dizzy spell or a fall.

**Does DHM help if I drink after donating blood?**

There is no good evidence that DHM reduces the dizziness or fainting risk after blood donation, and it doesn't replace the fluid, food, and time your body needs. The simple answer is to wait 24 hours before drinking. DHM research focuses on alcohol metabolism and hangovers, mostly in animal studies with limited human data.
